senses.def: a territory around the city of Abila, northwest of Damascus and ruled over by Lysanias
to engage in intense struggle, involving physical or nonphysical force against strong opposition
senses.comment: In a number of languages a marked distinction is made between physical fighting and nonphysical contending with someone. It is therefore often impossible to carry over any terminology involving war or physical struggling to contexts in which one is speaking of interpersonal hostility or contention.

senses.def: a race involving competition and struggle
act of speaking of the excellence of a person, object, or event
senses.comment: In a number of languages praise can only be expressed by direct discourse, and this requires some content which provides the basis for praise. For example, in Luke 2:13 instead of a literal rendering of ‘praising God,’ it may be necessary to have ‘they said, God is wonderful,’ and in Luke 16:8 it may be necessary to translate ‘the master of this dishonest manager said, You are remarkable for having done such a clever thing.’

senses.def: the best part of the booty, particularly that which is offered to deity
pertaining to not having a witness
senses.comment: In Acts 14:17 it may be rather difficult to introduce what is essentially a double negative, implied by ‘not’ and ‘without.’ Accordingly, Acts 14:17 may be rendered as ‘by the good things he does, everyone can know about him from experience.’

senses.def: to try to learn the location of something by searching for it (presumably somewhat more emphatic or goal-directed than in the case of ζητέω[a] ‘to try to learn where something is,’ 27.41)
glosses: to try to find out by looking for

senses.def: to conduct oneself, with apparent focus upon overt daily behavior
to rebuild something which has been destroyed
pertaining to that which or one who fails to reflect formal instruction or training
to journey away from one’s home or home country, implying for a considerable period of time and at quite a distance
glosses: to leave home on a journey
to be away from home on a journey

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to have a strong dislike for someone or something, implying repulsion and desire for avoidance
pertaining to not being wise
one who has personally seen an event and thus has personal knowledge and can be expected to attest to the occurrence of such an event
to cause or to let fall down
to move down suddenly and quickly
senses.comment: In a number of languages, however, it may be more appropriate to speak of a strong wind ‘blowing down from the island.’

senses.def: to cause a liquid to pour
to put or place some object or mass in a location, with the possible implication of force in some contexts
to cause a state or condition, with focus upon the suddenness or force of the action
to cause a state to cease by force and with the implication of elimination
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is extremely difficult to speak of states such as love and fear as being respectively agent and affected element. Therefore, it may be necessary to shift significantly the semantic structure so as to translate this expression in 1 John 4:18 as ‘if one completely loves, he does not at all fear.’

senses.def: to deposit money with a banker, with the intent of earning interest
(an idiom, literally: to throw on a bed) to cause someone to become very ill
(an idiom, literally: to throw into the heart) to cause someone to think in a particular manner, often as a means of inducing some behavior
(an idiom, literally: to throw a sickle) to begin to harvest a crop by cutting ripe grain with a sickle
senses.comment: In Revelation 14:16 and Revelation 14:19 this idiom occurs in a figurative context, and therefore it may be necessary in some languages to speak of ‘harvesting’ rather than using a phrase which mentions the literal use of a sickle.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to throw fire) to cause discord and contention
senses.comment: Some translators have preferred to retain the literal rendering of this expression in Luke 12:49, since this seems to be necessary in view of the larger figurative context, which speaks of ‘how I wish it were already kindled’ (τί θέλω εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη). A strictly literal translation may, however, be understood in a completely physical sense, namely, ‘to set the world on fire.’ There are a number of quite diverse interpretations of the significance of this expression in Luke 12:49. Some have assumed, for example, that it refers to the fire of Pentecost.

senses.def: rain, whether light or torrential
senses.comment: Though most languages have a general term for rain, the event of raining is more frequently referred to by a verb rather than by a noun, since rain is something which takes place and is not regarded as a thing or mass, unless, of course, one is referring to the water which comes down as rain, that is to say, ‘rain water’ (see 2.10). In some languages the event of raining is generally expressed idiomatically as ‘God is urinating.’ This might appear unduly crude and anthropomorphic, but to the speakers of such a language the expression is often quite acceptable and has no undesirable connotations.|Though in English one may use an impersonal subject with the verb ‘to rain,’ for example, ‘it is raining,’ many languages require some kind of personal agent, for example, ‘God is raining,’ or an impersonal agent such as ‘the sky is raining’ or ‘the clouds are raining.’

senses.def: to cause rain to fall
senses.comment: In a number of languages one cannot say literally ‘to send rain,’ for this would seem to imply that someone was carrying the rain to some destination. It may be more appropriate, therefore, to speak of ‘causing rain to fall’ or ‘causing rain to come down.’ It may be necessary, however, in some languages to indicate whether the occurrence of rain is for the detriment or the benefit of persons involved, and therefore it may be necessary to say in some instances ‘to cause rain to come down upon for the benefit of’; otherwise the reader might infer that the rain was some kind of punishment.

senses.def: to make something wet or moist
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made in the use of terms which imply different quantities of moisture, and one must make certain that the choice of a term in Luke 7:38 is in keeping with this context of crying and moistening by means of tears.

senses.def: (derivative of Γέρασα ‘Gerasa,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who lives in or is a native of Gerasa, a city in Peraea, east of the Jordan

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: one of the five long and slender projections of the human hand, used for writing, pointing, grasping, and other activities
senses.comment: Though it may seem quite logical to speak of ‘writing with the finger’ (John 8:6), in some languages one is required to speak of ‘writing with the hand.’ Similarly, in Matthew 23:4 the idiom ‘to lift a finger’ is more satisfactorily expressed as ‘to lift a hand.’ Expressions such as ‘to lift the hand’ and ‘to lift the finger’ must be carefully studied for their idiomatic significance, for ‘to lift the hand’ may mean ‘to release something,’ while ‘to lift the finger’ may be a lewd gesture.|In a number of languages the expression ‘to lift a finger’ (Matthew 23:4) may be best rendered as ‘to do a thing to help’ or ‘to help in any way.’ For δάκτυλος θεοῦ ‘the finger of God’ (Luke 11:20), see 76.3.

senses.def: power as an expression of the activity of a person or supernatural being
senses.comment: In some languages there is no abstract term for ‘power.’ The equivalent of doing something by the power of someone is ‘someone makes it possible to do’ or, in a figurative sense, ‘someone gives strength to do.’

senses.def: to tie objects together, or tie something around something else
to confine someone by binding with ropes or chains
senses.comment: ‘To imprison a person’ is often expressed in somewhat idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to be tied inside’ or ‘to be locked in the dark’ or even ‘to eat one’s food with rats.’

senses.def: to compel someone to act in a particular manner
senses.comment: In some instances ἀναγκάζω and δέω[c] may be rendered as ‘to cause it to be necessary for.’ In other instances a simple causative seems to be the closest equivalent. For example, the last clause of Galatians 2:14 may be expressed as ‘how can you make Gentiles live like Jews,’ and in Acts 20:22 one may translate ‘and now the Spirit makes me go to Jerusalem.’

senses.def: to cause someone to be under the authority of someone or something else
to exercise authority over something on the basis that it is not legitimate
senses.comment: There are a number of different interpretations of the implication of this statement in Matthew 16:19, and translators should carefully review this passage in various commentaries.

senses.def: to cause physical incapacity for someone
to complete an activity, normally involving movement
senses.comment: For another interpretation of διανύω in Acts 21:7, see 68.18.

senses.def: to continue, with the implication of movement
senses.comment: For another interpretation of διανύω in Acts 21:7, see 68.25.

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: two currents which meet in a body of water
senses.comment: Other scholars, however, interpret διθάλασσος together with τόπος as being a reef, a sandbar, or even a headland (see 1.68).|Cross-currents may be spoken of as ‘streams in the sea’ or ‘rivers in the sea’ or ‘two rivers that meet in the sea.’ It would be wrong, however, to use the expression ‘two rivers that meet in the sea’ if this meant merely two rivers which meet at the coastline as they flow from the interior. In this context ‘rivers’ can only refer to ‘rivers of the sea,’ in other words, ‘currents.’

senses.subdomain: Land in Contrast With the Sea
senses.def: a bar or reef produced in an area where two currents meet
senses.comment: It is possible to understand τόπος διθάλασσος in Acts 27:41 as a place of crosscurrents; see 14.32. In some languages it may be necessary to construct a descriptive equivalent for ‘sandbank,’ for example, ‘a hill of sand just beneath the surface of the water’ or ‘a ridge of sand hidden by the water.’

senses.def: to prepare or make something available for service
to bring serious charges or accusations against someone, with the possible connotation of a legal or court context
to carry or bring something into an area or structure
to cause someone to enter into a particular event or state
(an idiom, literally: to bring into the ears) to cause someone to hear
senses.comment: In a number of languages, however, it is awkward to speak of ‘to cause to hear’; rather, it seems far better to use an expression of ‘speaking,’ for example, ‘what we hear you say is strange.’ For another interpretation of this idiom in Acts 17:20, see 33.92.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to bring into the ears) to bring something to the attention of people by means of speech, but probably not in a formal or open manner
glosses: to bring to the attention of
senses.comment: For another interpretation of this idiom in Acts 17:20, see 24.55.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a point of time preceding another point of time, with an interval of considerable length
senses.comment: References to a point of time preceding another point of time may express a relationship to an event in the discourse or to the time of the discourse itself. In Hebrews 1:1 πάλαι[a] marks a point of time long before the actual writing of this Letter to the Hebrews. The same is true of ἔκπαλαι in 2 Peter 3:5. In some languages it is necessary to indicate clearly whether the interval is (1) between a prior time and the event mentioned in the discourse or (2) between a prior time and the discourse itself. For example, in Hebrews 1:1 it may be necessary to translate ‘long ago before now God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets’ or ‘long ago before now that I am writing …’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: an extensive period of time from a point in the past
(derivative of ἐλεύθερος[a] ‘free,’ 37.134) to cause someone to be set free or to be released
any creature living in the sea
senses.comment: In James 3:7 one may, of course, simply employ ‘fish,’ since these are the most prominent examples of creatures in the sea.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the inhabitants of a particular place
senses.comment: A typical rendering of ‘the local people’ is simply ‘the people who lived there’ or ‘those who inhabited that place.’

senses.def: to be a financial burden to someone by requiring too much support
glosses: to be a financial burden to

senses.def: to throw or hurl something upon something else
(an idiom, literally: to throw upon or to cast upon) to cause responsibility for something to be upon someone
senses.comment: For another explanation of this expression in 1 Peter 5:7, taking τὴν μέριμναν ἐπιρίπτω ἐπί as an idiom, see 25.250.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to cast cares upon) to stop worrying and to put one’s trust in someone
senses.comment: For another explanation of this expression in 1 Peter 5:7, taking only ἐπιρίπτω ἐπί as an idiom, see 90.18.

senses.def: (derivative of ἐργάζομαι[a] ‘to work,’ 42.41) engaging in some type of activity or behavior
involved in business, with focus upon the work which is involved
making a profit from one’s business or activity
(derivative of εὐεργετέω ‘to do good to,’ 88.7) a person who provides important help or assistance, often occurring as a title for princes or distinguished persons
to speak to or to make requests of God
senses.comment: In some languages there are a number of different terms used for prayer depending upon the nature of the content, for example, requests for material blessing, pleas for spiritual help, intercession for others, thanksgiving, and praise. There may also be important distinctions on the basis of urgency and need. The most generic expression for prayer may simply be ‘to speak to God.’ It is normally best to avoid an expression which means primarily ‘to recite.’

senses.def: to desire something, with the implication of a pious wish
fragrant plant (genus Mentha); up to 2 m high; small, soft leaves with sawlike margins; used in cooking, tea, medicine
senses.comment: In designating ‘mint’ as well as ἄνηθον ‘dill,’ πήγανον ‘rue,’ and κύμινον ‘cumin,’ it is probably wise to borrow a term and use a classifier, for example, ‘a seasoning herb called mint.’

senses.def: (derivative of θέλω[c] ‘to desire,’ 25.1) that which is desired or wished for

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: (derivative of θέλω[a] ‘to purpose,’ 30.58) that which is purposed, intended, or willed
(an idiom, literally: desire of the flesh) desire for sexual gratification
to burn aromatic substances as an offering to God

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
senses.def: leather strap or thong (used in binding sandals or shoes and as thongs in a whip)
senses.comment: In a number of languages ἱμάς[a] may be translated as ‘leather string’ or ‘strip of leather.’ In John 1:27 the term may be absorbed within the total expression, for example, worthy to untie his sandals (implying the untying of the straps with which the sandals were bound).|In Acts 22:25 the clause ὡς δὲ προέτειναν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἱμᾶσιν may be interpreted as ‘they tied him up with thongs’ or as ‘they tied him up for whipping,’ in which case ἱμᾶσιν would refer to an event, not to an object (see 19.9).

senses.def: act of beating severely with a whip
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἱμάς in Acts 22:25 as the thongs with which Paul was tied up (see 6.20).

senses.def: a brother of Jesus; see Ἰωσήφ[d]
a brother of James the younger
a tall straight grass or sedge; growing in or near rivers and marshes
the stalk of a reed plant
senses.comment: In some discussions of κάλαμος[b] the meaning is given as cane, but the term cane must not be confused with the meaning of walking stick. In Mark 15:19 it may be important in some languages to use a phrase such as heavy reed or strong reed, in order to avoid the impression that the instrument used in striking Jesus was some flimsy or fragile stalk of a plant.

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: a reed especially cut for making marks with ink on writing material; abou 20 cm long, sharpened on one end
a rod (possibly a reed) used for measuring length
senses.comment: There is no indication as to the particular length of κάλαμος[d], but it could have been as much as two meters (about seven feet), since this would not have been an unusual length for a reed. The equivalent of κάλαμος[d] may be simply ‘a measuring stick’ or ‘a stick with which to count the distance.’

senses.def: to break into pieces, implying thoroughness of the activity (in contrast with κλάω, 19.34)
behavior or conduct, with focus upon the demeanor of an individual

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to be in a lying or reclining position
to be in a place, frequently in the sense of ‘being contained in’ or ‘resting on’
to exist, with the implication of having been established and thus having continuity and purpose

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: a good reputation as an index of status

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: fecal matter used as agricultural fertilizer
act of making or creating something which has not existed before
glosses: creation (in the NT, used exclusively of God’s activity in creation)

senses.def: that which has been created
the universe as the product of God’s activity in creation
senses.comment: The meaning of κτίσις[c] might very well be treated as a simple derivative of the verb κτίζω ‘to create’ (42.35), since the reference is to the result of God’s creative act. However, in a number of contexts, the process of creation is no longer focal, and what is in focus is the total physical universe. In some languages the meaning may be best expressed as ‘the world and all that is in it’ or even ‘everything that exists.’

senses.def: (derivative of κτίζω ‘to create,’ 42.35) a human institution or social structure as something which has been created
senses.comment: It is possible that κτίσις in 1 Peter 2:13 may have the implication of authorized institution. It might even be possible to render κτίσις in such a context as ‘authority’ (compare κτίσις[e] in 37.43).

senses.def: an instituted authority, with the implication that such an authority has been created or formed
senses.comment: The expression ‘human authority’ may be rendered as ‘every person who has the right to rule.’ For another interpretation of κτίσις in 1 Peter 2:13, see 42.39.

senses.def: to perform religious rites as a part of worship
a widespread contagious disease, often associated with divine retribution
(a figurative extension of meaning of λοιμός[a] plague, 23.158) one who causes all sorts of trouble
pertaining to being soft to the touch

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the passive male partner in homosexual intercourse
senses.comment: For a context of μαλακός[b], see 1 Corinthians 6:9 in 88.280. As in Greek, a number of other languages also have entirely distinct terms for the active and passive roles in homosexual intercourse.

senses.def: an island located south of Sicily

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to be gentle in one’s attitude toward someone

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of μοιχεύω ‘to commit adultery,’ 88.276) a person who commits adultery, specifically referring to males, but also including females in generic contexts
a young man beyond the age of puberty, but normally before marriage
pertaining to ability to reason and hence understand
the surface of the earth as the dwelling place of mankind, in contrast with the heavens above and the world below
senses.comment: In Hebrews 2:5 there is a reference to τὴν οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν ‘the world to come, the future world.’ This has generally been interpreted as being equivalent to ‘the coming age,’ but the use of οἰκουμένη would seem to imply an inhabited world.

senses.def: the Roman Empire, including its inhabitants (οἰκουμένη[b] differs from οἰκουμένη[a] ‘earth,’ 1.39, in that those outside of the Roman Empire are specifically excluded, that is to say, no census was to be taken of the barbarians, but only of the inhabitants of the Empire)
senses.comment: In order to represent accurately the meaning of οἰκουμένη[b] in Luke 2:1 it may be possible to translate ‘Emperor Augustus sent out an order that all the people over whom he ruled should register themselves for the census.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of οἰκουμένη[a] ‘inhabited earth,’ 1.39) all people who dwell on the earth
the proper name of a person or object
(a figurative extension of meaning of ὄνομα[a] ‘name,’ 33.126) a person, with the possible implication of existence or relevance as individuals
senses.comment: In some instances ἄνθρωπος[a] ‘people’ (9.1) occurs together with ὄνομα[b] without any significant distinction in meaning (e.g. Revelation 11:13). See also 9.20.

senses.def: that which is said about a person on the basis of an evaluation of the person’s conduct
senses.comment: In obtaining a satisfactory equivalent for ‘reputation,’ it may be necessary to restructure considerably the clause in which a term such as μαρτυρία[c] or ὄνομα[c] occurs. For example, in 1 Timothy 3:7 one may translate ‘he should be the kind of man that people outside the church say is a good person.’ Similarly, in Revelation 3:1 one may need to translate ‘people speak of you as being alive even though you are dead.’

senses.def: category or kind, based upon an implied designation for a class of entities
(an idiom, literally: to name the name of the Lord) to employ the name of the Lord as evidence that one worships the Lord
glosses: to say that one belongs to the Lord or to declare that one is a worshiper of the Lord

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to throw out the name) to insult or slander, with a possible implication of a kind of psychological ostracism

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the part of the human body above the hips and below the ribs, the customary place for tying a belt
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘waist’ is a term meaning literally ‘the middle.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the male genital organs (‘loins’ in traditional English translations)
senses.comment: A literal rendering of ‘he was still in the genitals of his father’ (Hebrews 7:10) might be regarded in a number of languages as being excessively specific and even vulgar. It is possible to render this passage as simply ‘he was not as yet born’ or ‘his father had not yet caused him to be conceived.’ In Acts 2:30 (καρποῦ τῆς ὀσφύος αὐτοῦ ‘the fruit of his loins’) it may be best to translate ‘one of his descendants’ (see 10.34).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to gird up the loins) to cause oneself to be in a state of readiness
senses.comment: In the context of Ephesians 6:14, however, it may be useful to preserve the extended figure of readiness for warfare beginning with Ephesians 6:13 and extending through verse 17.

senses.def: to strike or hit an object, one or more times
to sting (as of a scorpion)
pertaining to being lame and/or paralyzed
senses.comment: It is often best to speak of a paralytic as ‘one who cannot walk.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to be provoked or upset at someone or something involving severe emotional concern
senses.comment: In some languages the expression ‘to be greatly upset’ must be rendered idiomatically as ‘his heart was eating him’ or ‘his stomach was hot.’

senses.def: an important city in northwest Asia Minor
bedrock (possibly covered with a thin layer of soil), rocky crags, or mountain ledges, in contrast with separate pieces of rock normally referred to as λίθος[a] (see 2.23)
senses.comment: ὁμοιωθήσεται ἀνδρὶ φρονίμῳ, ὅστις ᾠκοδόμησεν αὐτοῦ τὴν οἰκίαν ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν ‘he is like a wise man who built his house on bedrock’ Matthew 7:24; ἔθηκεν αὐτὸν ἐν μνημείῳ ὅ ἦν λελατομημένον ἐκ πέτρας ‘they then put him in a grave which had been hewn from rock’ Mark 15:46; λέγουσιν τοῖς ὄρεσιν καὶ ταῖς πέτραις, Πέσετε ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς ‘they said to the mountains and to the rock cliffs, Fall on us’ Revelation 6:16. In these three contexts πέτρα must be translated in some languages by three quite different terms. Bedrock, that is to say, the rock which lies horizontally and often just below the surface, may be referred to by one term, while rock with an exposed face into which a tomb could be hewn would be quite different. Similarly, the rocks which would be called upon to fall upon people would be rendered by a term referring to ‘cliffs’ or ‘precipices.’|In Luke 8:6 the term πέτρα in ἕτερον κατέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν ‘other (seed) fell on rocky ground’ refers to bedrock which may be covered with a thin layer of soil. One may translate such an expression as ‘thin ground over rock’ or ‘just a little soil on top of rock.’|In those passages which involve a play on words with the name Πέτρος ‘Peter,’ πέτρα refers to bedrock, that is to say, the rock on which a foundation may be placed.

senses.def: a quantity which fills a space
a total quantity, with emphasis upon completeness
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to use a generic expression such as ‘totality.’ As a result, this clause in Colossians 2:9 must often be completely restructured, for example, ‘for Christ is completely like God’ or ‘for just what God is, that is exactly what Christ is.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: the totality of a period of time, with the implication of proper completion

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to engage in sexual immorality of any kind, often with the implication of prostitution
senses.comment: In some NT contexts πορνεία may refer specifically to incest.

senses.def: a person several preceding generations removed from the reference person
senses.comment: In a number of languages one’s forefathers may be referred to simply as ‘fathers who have long since died.’ In other languages they may be referred to as ‘fathers of other generations’ or ‘fathers of ancient times.’

senses.def: to expect something to happen, whether good or bad
an utterance inspired by God
senses.comment: It is possible that προφητεία in 1 Corinthians 13:8 refers to the action of producing such inspired utterances rather than to the resulting verbal form of the utterances themselves.

senses.def: the capacity or ability to utter inspired messages
glosses: to be able to speak inspired messages

senses.def: a marker of negative purpose, often with the implication of apprehension

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a member of a politically influential Jewish party in Jerusalem at the time of Jesus and the apostles. The Sadducees were a smaller group than the Pharisees (see 11.49), but were often in control of important political and religious positions. Their denial of the resurrection of the dead and their acceptance of only the first five books of the OT are important elements in some of the important differences which arose between the Sadducees and the Pharisees
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
that toward which movement or activity is directed
senses.comment: The context of σκοπός in Philippians 3:14 is highly figurative, and in some languages it may be better rendered as ‘what I seek to achieve’ or ‘what I wish to accomplish.’ For σκοπός in the idiom κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω, see 89.56.

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Punishment and Execution
senses.def: a pole stuck into the ground in an upright position with a crosspiece attached to its upper part; used as a means of execution
senses.comment: In Matthew 27:32 (τοῦτον ἠγγάρευσαν ἵνα ἄρῃ τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ ‘they forced him to carry Jesus’ cross’) the reference is probably to the crosspiece of the cross, which normally would have been carried by a man condemned to die.|Because of the symbolism associated with the cross, translations of the NT in all languages preserve some expression which will identify the cross, not only as a means of capital punishment, but as having a particular form, namely, an upright pole with a crossbeam. In some receptor languages the term for a cross means simply ‘crossbeam.’ In other instances it is composed of a phrase meaning ‘crossed poles.’ It is important, however, to avoid an expression which will suggest crossed sticks in the form of X rather than a cross consisting of an upright with a horizontal beam. If at all possible one should employ a term or phrase which may be used in an extended sense, since in so many contexts the term ‘cross’ refers not only to the instrument of Christ’s death, but to the event of execution. It also becomes a symbol of the message of forgiveness and of reconciliation. Because of these extended meanings, it is important to choose a form which can, if at all possible, support these additional meanings.

senses.def: to undergo the same type of suffering as others do
glosses: to assume one’s share of suffering

senses.def: to send someone together with someone else
senses.comment: In some languages it may be difficult to express in a succinct way the meaning of ‘to send with.’ For example, in 2 Corinthians 8:22 it may be necessary to translate ‘they are going and so we are causing our Christian brother to go with them,’ and in 2 Corinthians 12:18 one may translate ‘I begged Titus to go, and I caused the other Christian brother to go with him.’

senses.def: to eat together with others
senses.comment: In a number of languages a term meaning ‘to eat together with others’ is completely distinct from an expression referring to eating by one person. Furthermore, a term meaning basically ‘to eat together’ may focus primarily on conviviality and feasting rather than merely on the process of eating. In Acts 11:3 there is no indication of ‘feasting.’

senses.def: to slaughter, either animals or persons; in contexts referring to persons, the implication is of violence and mercilessness
a particularly strong permanent wall, primarily the wall built around a city for its protection
senses.comment: In a number of languages a translator must make a clear distinction between a wall of a house and a city wall. The wall of a house may be called ‘a side of a house’ and an inner wall ‘a partition in a house,’ while a city wall is often related to terms such as ‘barricade’ or ‘fence.’ Hence, a city wall may be called ‘a fortified fence around a city.’

senses.def: a Jewish proselyte in Corinth whose additional name was Justus; see 93.179
to be of surpassing or exceptional value
to exercise continuous control over someone or something
senses.comment: There is usually no difficulty in speaking of ‘control’ if it is performed by a person as in 1 Peter 2:13. However, it may not be possible to speak of ‘death’ having control, unless the language in question can personify death. In some instances Acts 2:24 (see 37.16) must be rendered as ‘it was impossible for him to continue to be dead,’ and in 2 Corinthians 5:14 ‘Christ’s love controls us’ may be rendered as ‘the fact that Christ loves us causes us to act as we do.’

a marker of negatively linked elements
senses.comment: It would be wrong to restructure John 1:3 to read ‘he made everything in all creation,’ for in the Scriptures God is spoken of as the Creator, but the creation was done ‘through the Word.’ If one must restructure John 1:3, it may be possible to say ‘he was involved in everything that was created’ or ‘he took part in creating everything.’|In 1 Corinthians 11:11 χωρίς does not specify the particular relationship but only indicates the lack of relationship or involvement. This, of course, is negated by οὔτε, so that one may translate this portion of 1 Corinthians 11:11 as ‘nor is woman without some relationship to man, nor is man without relationship to woman.’ In view of the overall context, one may then render the passage simply as ‘woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman.’ In some languages, however, it may be necessary of ‘wife’ and ‘husband,’ since terms for ‘man’ or ‘woman’ may be wrongly interpreted in a strictly erotic sense.|Because of the double negation of 1 Corinthians 11:11, in some languages it may be necessary to employ a positive equivalent, for example, ‘for woman is dependent on man and man is dependent on woman’ or ‘a wife is dependent on her husband and a husband is dependent on his wife.’|The expression ‘apart from any works’ in Romans 4:6 may be rendered in some languages as ‘and what a person does, does not count’ or ‘and this is not because of what one does.’
